blocks.body:
Stand $20$ metres from a tree and look at its top: your line of sight makes an angle of $35^\circ$ with the ground. That is enough to know the height of the tree, about $14$ metres. This link between angles and lengths is trigonometry.

The same functions describe anything that goes round or back and forth, like a wheel or a sound wave. To cover those we extend sine and cosine to all real numbers using a point moving around a circle, and prove the addition formulas, from which nearly every other identity follows.

blocks.title: Right triangles
blocks.body:
Take a right triangle with an acute angle $\theta$. Call the side opposite $\theta$ the opposite side, the other short side the adjacent side, and the longest side the hypotenuse. Two right triangles with the same angle $\theta$ have the same three angles, so they are similar ([[euclid-basics]]) and their side ratios agree. So these ratios depend only on $\theta$:
$$\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.$$
Two triangles give exact values. Half a square, with legs $1$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt 2$, has two $45^\circ$ angles, so $\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}$. Half an equilateral triangle of side $2$ has hypotenuse $2$, legs $1$ and $\sqrt 3$, and angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; so $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 30^\circ = \sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}$.

For the tree, the height $h$ satisfies $\tan 35^\circ = h/20$, so $h = 20\tan 35^\circ \approx 20 \times 0.700 = 14.0$ metres.

blocks.title: Radians and the unit circle
blocks.body:
Degrees are a convention. The natural measure of an angle is arc length: draw a circle of radius $1$ around the vertex, and the size of the angle is the length of the arc it cuts off. This is radian measure. The whole circle has circumference $2\pi$, so
$$360^\circ = 2\pi, \qquad 180^\circ = \pi, \qquad 90^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \qquad 60^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \qquad 45^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{4}, \qquad 30^\circ = \tfrac{\pi}{6},$$
and one radian is $180^\circ/\pi \approx 57.3^\circ$. From now on angles are in radians unless a degree sign is shown.

Now walk anticlockwise a distance $\theta$ along the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, starting at $(1, 0)$. If $0 < \theta < \pi/2$, dropping a perpendicular from the point reached to the $x$-axis gives a right triangle with hypotenuse $1$ and angle $\theta$ at the origin, so the point is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. We make this the definition for every $\theta$.

blocks.title: Sine and cosine
blocks.body:
For every real number $\theta$, let $P(\theta)$ be the point reached by travelling a distance $\theta$ along the unit circle from $(1, 0)$, anticlockwise for positive $\theta$ and clockwise for negative $\theta$. Then $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ are the coordinates of this point:
$$P(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta).$$
Also $\tan\theta = \sin\theta / \cos\theta$ whenever $\cos\theta \ne 0$.

So cosine and sine are the horizontal and vertical positions of a point moving around the unit circle at unit speed.

blocks.title: First properties
blocks.body:
Several facts can be read straight off the circle.

1. $P(\theta)$ is on the unit circle, so $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$; both values lie in $[-1, 1]$.
2. An extra $2\pi$ brings you back to the same point: $\sin(\theta + 2\pi) = \sin\theta$ and $\cos(\theta + 2\pi) = \cos\theta$. Both functions have period $2\pi$.
3. Walking $-\theta$ gives the mirror image of $P(\theta)$ in the $x$-axis: $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$ and $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$. Cosine is even and sine is odd ([[functions]]).
4. An extra $\pi$ takes you to the opposite point: $\sin(\theta + \pi) = -\sin\theta$ and $\cos(\theta + \pi) = -\cos\theta$. Hence $\tan$ has period $\pi$.
5. Reflection in the line $y = x$ swaps the coordinates, sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1) = P(\pi/2)$ and reverses the direction of travel, so it sends $P(\theta)$ to $P(\pi/2 - \theta)$. Hence $\cos(\tfrac\pi2 - \theta) = \sin\theta$ and $\sin(\tfrac\pi2 - \theta) = \cos\theta$.

The two triangles and these symmetries give the special values:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} \theta & 0 & \frac{\pi}{6} & \frac{\pi}{4} & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{\pi}{2} & \frac{2\pi}{3} & \pi & \frac{3\pi}{2} & 2\pi \\ \hline \sin\theta & 0 & \frac12 & \frac{\sqrt2}{2} & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & 1 & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ \cos\theta & 1 & \frac{\sqrt3}{2} & \frac{\sqrt2}{2} & \frac12 & 0 & -\frac12 & -1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}$$
The graph of $\sin$ is a wave of period $2\pi$ between $-1$ and $1$. The graph of $\cos$ is the same wave moved left by $\pi/2$, since $\cos\theta = \sin(\theta + \tfrac\pi2)$ (fact 5 applied to $-\theta$, with fact 3).

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Rotate the plane about the origin clockwise by arc length $\beta$. This maps the unit circle to itself and moves each point $P(\theta)$ to $P(\theta - \beta)$; in particular $P(\beta)$ goes to $P(0) = (1, 0)$ and $P(\alpha)$ goes to $P(\alpha - \beta)$. Rotations do not change distances, so the distance from $P(\alpha)$ to $P(\beta)$ equals the distance from $P(\alpha - \beta)$ to $P(0)$. Compute the squares of both with the distance formula, using $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$:
$$(\cos\alpha - \cos\beta)^2 + (\sin\alpha - \sin\beta)^2 = 2 - 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta),$$
$$\big(\cos(\alpha - \beta) - 1\big)^2 + \sin^2(\alpha - \beta) = 2 - 2\cos(\alpha - \beta).$$
Setting these equal gives the first formula. Replacing $\beta$ by $-\beta$, and using $\cos(-\beta) = \cos\beta$ and $\sin(-\beta) = -\sin\beta$, gives the second.

For sine, use fact 5 above, $\cos(\tfrac\pi2 - x) = \sin x$ and $\sin(\tfrac\pi2 - x) = \cos x$, together with the first formula:
$$\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\big((\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha) - \beta\big) = \cos(\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha)\cos\beta + \sin(\tfrac\pi2 - \alpha)\sin\beta = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta.$$
Replacing $\beta$ by $-\beta$ gives the last formula.

blocks.title: Consequences: double angles and triangles
blocks.body:
Putting $\beta = \alpha$ gives the double-angle formulas
$$\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha, \qquad \cos 2\alpha = \cos^2\alpha - \sin^2\alpha = 2\cos^2\alpha - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2\alpha.$$
Solved for $\cos^2\alpha$ and $\sin^2\alpha$, the last two read $\cos^2\alpha = \tfrac{1 + \cos 2\alpha}{2}$ and $\sin^2\alpha = \tfrac{1 - \cos 2\alpha}{2}$, which let you halve angles. For example $\cos^2\tfrac\pi8 = \tfrac12\big(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\big)$, so $\cos\tfrac\pi8 = \tfrac12\sqrt{2 + \sqrt 2}$.

Back to triangles. In a triangle $ABC$ write $a = BC$, $b = CA$, $c = AB$, and let $C$ also denote the angle at $C$. Place $C$ at the origin and $A$ at $(b, 0)$, with $B$ above the $x$-axis. Then $B$ is at distance $a$ from the origin in the direction at angle $C$ to the positive $x$-axis: $B = (a\cos C, a\sin C)$. The distance formula gives the law of cosines:
$$c^2 = (a\cos C - b)^2 + a^2\sin^2 C = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C.$$
When $C = \pi/2$ this is Pythagoras' theorem. The same coordinates show that the height from $B$ is $a\sin C$, so the area is $\tfrac12 ab\sin C$. Writing the area in the three possible ways and dividing by $\tfrac12 abc$ gives the law of sines:
$$\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c}.$$

blocks.title: Exact values
blocks.solution:
Write $15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ$ and use the subtraction formulas:
$$\cos 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4}, \qquad \sin 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} - \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt6 - \sqrt2}{4}.$$
Then
$$\tan 15^\circ = \frac{\sqrt6 - \sqrt2}{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2} = \frac{(\sqrt6 - \sqrt2)^2}{6 - 2} = \frac{8 - 2\sqrt{12}}{4} = 2 - \sqrt3.$$
As a sanity check, $\cos 15^\circ \approx 0.9659$, close to $1$ as it should be for a small angle.

blocks.title: A trigonometric equation
blocks.body: Find all $x$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ with $2\sin^2 x - \sin x - 1 = 0$.
blocks.solution:
This is a quadratic in $s = \sin x$: $2s^2 - s - 1 = (2s + 1)(s - 1) = 0$. So $\sin x = 1$ or $\sin x = -\tfrac12$.

On the unit circle, $\sin x = 1$ only at the top, $x = \tfrac\pi2$. Height $-\tfrac12$ is reached at the mirror images in the $x$-axis of the points at $\tfrac\pi6$ and $\tfrac{5\pi}6$, that is, at $x = \tfrac{11\pi}{6}$ and $x = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}$.

The solutions are $\tfrac\pi2$, $\tfrac{7\pi}6$ and $\tfrac{11\pi}6$; on all of $\mathbb R$, add any multiple of $2\pi$ to these.

blocks.title: Adding two waves
blocks.body: Find the largest value of $3\sin x + 4\cos x$.
blocks.solution:
Factor out $5 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}$:
$$3\sin x + 4\cos x = 5\left(\tfrac35\sin x + \tfrac45\cos x\right).$$
Since $(\tfrac35)^2 + (\tfrac45)^2 = 1$, the point $(\tfrac35, \tfrac45)$ lies on the unit circle, so it is $P(\varphi)$ for some angle $\varphi$: $\cos\varphi = \tfrac35$ and $\sin\varphi = \tfrac45$. By the addition formula,
$$3\sin x + 4\cos x = 5(\sin x\cos\varphi + \cos x\sin\varphi) = 5\sin(x + \varphi).$$
This is at most $5$, and equals $5$ when $x = \tfrac\pi2 - \varphi$ (there $\sin x = \tfrac35$, $\cos x = \tfrac45$, and $3 \cdot \tfrac35 + 4 \cdot \tfrac45 = 5$). The maximum is $5$.

The same argument shows that $a\sin x + b\cos x$ is a single wave of amplitude $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

blocks.title: A product of cosines
blocks.solution:
Call the product $Q$ and put $s = \sin\tfrac\pi7$, which is not $0$. The angles double from one factor to the next, which suggests using $2\sin t\cos t = \sin 2t$ repeatedly:
$$8sQ = 4\Big(2\sin\tfrac\pi7\cos\tfrac\pi7\Big)\cos\tfrac{2\pi}7\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7 = 2\Big(2\sin\tfrac{2\pi}7\cos\tfrac{2\pi}7\Big)\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7 = 2\sin\tfrac{4\pi}7\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7 = \sin\tfrac{8\pi}7.$$
Now $\sin\tfrac{8\pi}{7} = \sin(\pi + \tfrac\pi7) = -\sin\tfrac\pi7 = -s$. So $8sQ = -s$, and dividing by $s \ne 0$ gives $Q = -\tfrac18$.

The same trick shows $\cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ\cos 80^\circ = \tfrac18$: there the last step gives $\sin 160^\circ = \sin 20^\circ$, with a plus sign.

blocks.body:
- Calculus formulas, such as the slope of $\sin$ at $0$ being $1$, hold only in radians; check your calculator's mode.
- $\sin(\alpha + \beta) \ne \sin\alpha + \sin\beta$ in general: with $\alpha = \beta = \pi/2$ the left side is $0$ and the right side is $2$.
- $\sin^2 x$ means $(\sin x)^2$, but $\sin^{-1}x$ usually means $\arcsin x$, not $1/\sin x$.
- $\sin x = \tfrac12$ has infinitely many solutions, $x = \tfrac\pi6 + 2k\pi$ and $x = \tfrac{5\pi}6 + 2k\pi$ for integers $k$; a calculator's $\arcsin$ returns only the one in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.
- Dividing an equation by $\sin x$ or $\cos x$ loses the solutions where it is zero. Factor instead: $\sin 2x = \sin x$ becomes $\sin x\,(2\cos x - 1) = 0$.

With complex numbers, $P(\theta)$ becomes $\cos\theta + i\sin\theta = e^{i\theta}$, and the addition formulas say that multiplying two such numbers adds their angles ([[complex-numbers]]). The dot product of two vectors is $|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta$, proved from the law of cosines above ([[vectors-plane]]). Comparing areas in the unit circle gives $\sin x / x \to 1$ ([[limits]]), from which $(\sin x)' = \cos x$ follows ([[diff-rules]]); then $\sin$ and $\cos$ solve $y'' = -y$, the equation of a vibrating spring ([[ode-linear]]).

Writing periodic functions as sums of sines and cosines is [[fourier-poisson]]. In olympiad geometry the laws of sines and cosines are standard tools ([[triangle-centres]]).
